lead: Every page is a pile of boxes, and CSS layout decides where each box sits. Normal flow stacks them, position lifts one out, Flexbox lines items along one axis, Grid builds rows and columns, and media queries rearrange the whole thing for a narrow screen. The same HTML document then serves a phone in a Chennai bus queue and a large office monitor. This chapter shows how each tool measures space, so you can predict the pixel widths before you open the browser.
prereq: You need: the box model from chapter 2.6 and selector and media-query syntax from chapter 2.5.

sections.h3: Normal flow, display and the position property

blocks.text: Before any CSS, boxes follow normal flow. Block boxes stack top to bottom and fill the parent's width; inline boxes sit side by side on a line. The display property changes this: block, inline, inline-block, flex, grid or none. display: none removes the box and its space; visibility: hidden hides the paint but keeps the space.

position sets how the browser places a box. static is the default and ignores top, right, bottom, left. relative shifts the box from its normal spot by those offsets but keeps the original space. absolute lifts the box out of flow and measures the offsets from its containing block: the nearest ancestor whose position is not static, or the page's initial containing block if there is none. fixed does the same against the viewport, so it stays put while the page scrolls. sticky acts relative until the box reaches a scroll threshold, then sticks inside its parent.

z-index decides which overlapping box paints on top. It works on positioned boxes and on flex and grid items; higher numbers win, and equal values fall back to source order. The old layout technique was float: left or right, with clear: both on the next element so it stops wrapping around the float. You will still see it in legacy code, but Flexbox and Grid replaced it.

sections.h3: Flexbox: one dimension at a time

blocks.text: Set display: flex on a container and its direct children become flex items arranged on one axis. flex-direction: row (the default) runs the main axis left to right; column runs it top to bottom. justify-content spreads items along the main axis (flex-start, center, flex-end, space-between, space-around, space-evenly). align-items places them across the cross axis: stretch is the default, and center, flex-start, flex-end, baseline are the alternatives. align-self overrides alignment for one item, flex-wrap: wrap lets items drop to a new line, and gap adds fixed space between items without margins.

Sizing uses three numbers. flex-basis is the item's starting size on the main axis, flex-grow is its share of leftover free space (default 0), and flex-shrink says how much it gives up when space is short (default 1). The shorthand flex: 1 means grow 1, shrink 1, basis 0, so the whole container counts as free space and splits by grow ratio.

blocks.where: W is the container's inner width in px; n is the number of items; g is the gap in px; growᵢ is that item's flex-grow; Σgrow is the sum of all grow values.

blocks.text: order: 2 moves an item later on the screen without touching the HTML. Screen readers and Tab order still follow the HTML source, so the visual and spoken sequences differ. Never use it to reorder content that has a meaningful sequence.

display: grid makes a two-dimensional container. grid-template-columns lists track sizes; grid-template-rows does the same downward. The fr unit is a share of the space left after fixed tracks and gaps, so grid-template-columns: 200px 1fr 2fr gives 200 px, then one third and two thirds of the rest. repeat(3, 1fr) means 1fr 1fr 1fr, and minmax(150px, 1fr) sets a floor of 150 px and lets the track grow freely above it, sharing the leftover space with the other fr tracks.

auto-fill and auto-fit both create as many tracks as fit; auto-fill keeps the empty ones, auto-fit collapses them so the items stretch. grid-template-areas draws the layout as strings of names, and each child claims a name with grid-area: header. Items can also be placed by line: grid-column: 1 / 3 spans the first two columns, and grid-column: span 2 does the same from wherever the item lands. gap separates tracks. Use Flexbox for a navbar or a row of buttons, Grid for the page skeleton.

sections.h3: Responsive design: one layout for every screen

blocks.text: Without help, a phone browser pretends the page is about 980 px wide and shrinks it. The viewport meta tag fixes that.

Responsive design means one HTML document and CSS that adapts. Mobile-first writes the small-screen rules as the base and adds larger ones inside @media (min-width: 768px) { ... }. Breakpoints are chosen where the content breaks, not by device names; 576, 768, 992 and 1200 px are common. Sizes use relative units — %, rem, em, vw — so text and boxes scale with the root font size or the screen.

Images get max-width: 100% and height: auto so they never overflow. srcset lists several files with width descriptors plus a sizes attribute; the browser picks the file whose width suits the space the image will occupy and the screen's pixel density. The picture element with a source media="(min-width: 768px)" child serves a different crop on wide screens. Test by dragging the browser narrow, not by trusting the CSS.

examples.question: A flex container is 600 px wide and holds three items with flex: 1, flex: 2 and flex: 1 and flex-basis 0. Find each item's width (a) when gap is 0 and (b) when gap: 30px is applied.
steps: Sum the grow values: 1 + 2 + 1 = 4, so the shares are 1/4, 2/4 and 1/4.
Case (b), gap 30 px: three items have two gaps between them, so total gap space = 2 × 30 = 60 px.
Check the total: 135 + 270 + 135 + 60 = 600 px, which matches the container.
examples.answer: With no gap the widths are 150 px, 300 px and 150 px; with a 30 px gap they become 135 px, 270 px and 135 px.
examples.check:
W = 600
gap = 30
shares = [1, 2, 1]
total = sum(shares)
n = len(shares)
free0 = W - 0
for s in shares:
    print(free0 * s / total)
free_g = W - (n - 1) * gap
for s in shares:
    print(free_g * s / total)

traps: position: absolute measures from the nearest ancestor that is not static, not from the page. If no ancestor is positioned, the box lands relative to the initial containing block. Give the parent position: relative.
flex: 1 is flex: 1 1 0, with basis zero, so widths follow the grow ratio, not the content. flex: auto is 1 1 auto, which starts from the content size and only distributes what is left.
A 1fr track is really minmax(auto, 1fr). A child with a min-width or one long unbroken word pushes the track wider and the grid overflows. Use minmax(0, 1fr) or overflow-wrap on the child.

z-index is ignored on an ordinary static box; it applies to positioned boxes and to flex and grid items. A child is trapped inside its parent's stacking context. A z-index: 9999 child still paints below any element outside that context that stacks above the parent, such as a sibling of the parent with a higher z-index.

Leave out the viewport meta tag and media queries fire at the wrong width on a phone. Also order matters: in mobile-first CSS, min-width queries must run from smallest to largest so later rules add, not cancel.

quiz.q: Name the five position values and say which is the default.
quiz.a: static (the default), relative, absolute, fixed, sticky.

quiz.q: State the difference between display: none and visibility: hidden.
quiz.a: display: none removes the box from the layout, so the space disappears and later boxes move up. visibility: hidden keeps the box and its space but does not paint it.

quiz.q: Which axis does justify-content act on, and which does align-items act on?
quiz.a: justify-content acts on the main axis, set by flex-direction (row by default, so horizontal). align-items acts on the cross axis (vertical for a row).

quiz.q: A grid container is 900 px wide with gap: 20px and grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr)). How many columns fit, and how wide is each?
quiz.a: n columns need 200n + 20(n − 1) ≤ 900, that is 220n ≤ 920, so n = 4. Track width = (900 − 3 × 20) ÷ 4 = 840 ÷ 4 = 210 px.

quiz.q: A flex container is 800 px wide with gap: 20px and two items of flex: 1 and flex: 3. Find the two widths.
quiz.a: Total grow = 4, one gap = 20 px, free space = 800 − 20 = 780 px. Widths are 780 × 1/4 = 195 px and 780 × 3/4 = 585 px. Check: 195 + 585 + 20 = 800 px.

quiz.q: A grid column is 1fr but the layout still overflows sideways because one cell holds a long unbroken URL. Explain why and give the fix.
quiz.a: 1fr means minmax(auto, 1fr), and auto sets the track minimum to the content's min-content size, which for an unbreakable word is the whole word. The track grows past its share. Fix with minmax(0, 1fr) on the track and overflow-wrap: anywhere on the cell.

quiz.q: Why is order risky on a list of form fields or a navigation bar?
quiz.a: order changes only the visual order. Keyboard Tab order and screen-reader order still follow the HTML, so sighted and non-sighted users experience different sequences, which confuses navigation. Reorder the HTML instead.

beyond: Not for the exam. Container queries (@container) let a component respond to its own width instead of the screen width, which suits reusable design systems. Subgrid lets a child grid reuse its parent's row or column tracks so nested cards line up. The clamp() function makes type fluid between a minimum and a maximum without a media query, aspect-ratio reserves space before an image loads, and cascade layers (@layer) settle conflicts between stylesheets. Search "CSS container queries", "subgrid" and "cascade layers" for the current state of these features.
